official_name: Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Alzheimer's Disease
plain_title: The most common cause of dementia
one_liner: A gradual, progressive decline in memory and thinking caused by Alzheimer's disease, the commonest cause of dementia.
in_simple_words: Alzheimer's disease is a brain condition that slowly damages nerve cells, usually starting with short-term memory: forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, misplacing things. Over years it spreads to language, finding the way, planning, and recognizing people. It's the cause of most dementia and mainly affects people over 65, though it can start earlier. There's no cure yet, but medications can ease symptoms, newer treatments can slow early disease for some, and support makes an enormous difference.
what_it_can_feel_like: Dad asks the same question five times and each time it's new to him. I've learned to answer each time as if it is.
I was diagnosed at 58. I'm still here, still me, doing what I can while I can.
The support group taught me how to be with my wife now, not just grieve who she was.
common_signs: Forgetting recent events and conversations; repeating questions
Trouble finding words, following conversations, or managing money
Difficulty with planning, judgment, and everyday tasks
Changes in mood, personality, or withdrawal
Gradual onset and slow, steady worsening over years

myths_vs_facts.myth: Alzheimer's and dementia are the same thing.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Dementia is the umbrella; Alzheimer's is the most common cause of it. Other causes have different patterns and treatments.

myths_vs_facts.myth: If a parent had it, I'll get it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most Alzheimer's isn't directly inherited. Family history raises risk somewhat; healthy heart, hearing, activity, and social life lower it.
Medication, newer disease-modifying treatments for some people, activity, support, and planning all change the course and quality of life.

how_common.plain: Alzheimer's disease causes around 6 to 7 in every 10 cases of dementia worldwide, affecting tens of millions of people, and risk rises sharply after 65.
how_common.figure: 60–70% of the 55 million people with dementia worldwide (WHO)

what_helps.plain_summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, can modestly ease symptoms. Newer antibody treatments that slow early Alzheimer's are approved in some countries for carefully selected people, with significant monitoring. Cognitive stimulation therapy, exercise, social activity, and treating hearing loss help. Behavioural and psychological symptoms are managed with non-drug approaches first. Carer support, dementia-friendly adjustments at home, and early planning are central.
evidence_based_options: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Disease-modifying antibody treatments for selected people with early disease, where approved
Cognitive stimulation therapy, exercise, and social engagement
Carer education, support groups, and advance care planning
self_help_that_supports_care: Routines, labels, and reminders at home
Staying active, social, and engaged in enjoyable activities
Carers: respite, support groups, and looking after their own health
Planning finances, care wishes, and legal arrangements early

when_to_reach_out: If memory problems are getting worse and affecting daily life, see a doctor for assessment. Early diagnosis gives access to treatment, support, and the chance to plan. Carers: ask for help before you're exhausted.
is_not: Normal age-related forgetfulness, memory problems from depression, medication, thyroid or vitamin problems, and other dementias are not Alzheimer's. Only assessment can tell.
hope_note: People live meaningful lives with Alzheimer's for years, and families find connection in new ways. Nobody has to face it alone.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.

in_young_people: Early-onset Alzheimer's (before 65) is rare but real and often misdiagnosed as stress or depression. Younger people need services designed for their stage of life, including work and family responsibilities.
across_cultures: Alzheimer's affects every community. Diagnosis comes later for people from minority and lower-income groups, and some languages have no word for dementia. Culturally adapted services and interpreters improve care.
